questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Tolu broke her leg because of her "restive" nature.

options.why: Lively means full of energy, which is milder than the hard-to-control quality of restive.
options.whyWrong: Lively usually sounds cheerful and active, whereas restive means restless and impatient under control.

options.why: Relaxed is the opposite of restive.
options.whyWrong: Relaxed means calm and at ease, which is the opposite of restive.

options.why: Patient means able to wait calmly, the opposite of restive.
options.whyWrong: Someone who is patient waits calmly, while a restive person is restless and hard to keep still.

options.why: Restive means restless, impatient and unwilling to be controlled, which matches unruly.

questions.hint: Watch out: restive does NOT come from 'resting' — it means impatient and hard to control.
questions.explanation: "Restive" means restless, impatient and difficult to control. In this sentence, Tolu's unruly behaviour led to her breaking her leg.
questions.trap: Option A (lively) is tempting, and many students confuse "restive" with "restful" (relaxed). Restive actually means restless and unruly.
questions.mnemonic: Restive = restless and unruly, NOT resting.

askPresets.answer: Think of a horse that refuses to stand still — it is restive, meaning unruly.
Lively means full of positive energy, whereas restive points to impatience and lack of self-control, which matches unruly.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The secretary's speech was interesting, though "impromptu".

options.why: Impromptu means done or spoken without earlier preparation.
Improper means unsuitable or rude, not unplanned.
options.whyWrong: Improper means wrong or inappropriate, which does not match impromptu.

options.why: Controversial means causing disagreement, which is unrelated to preparation.
options.whyWrong: Controversial is about sparking debate, not speaking without notes or rehearsal.

options.why: Important means of great value, not unplanned.
options.whyWrong: A speech can be important whether prepared or not; impromptu specifically means without preparation.

questions.hint: Look at the contrast word "though": the speech was interesting even though it was done on the spot.
questions.explanation: "Impromptu" describes something done or said on the spur of the moment without prior planning or rehearsal, so "unprepared" is nearest in meaning.
questions.trap: Option B sounds a little like "impromptu" because both start with "imp-", but "improper" means unsuitable, not unplanned.

askPresets.answer: If the principal calls you up to give a vote of thanks with zero notice, that is an impromptu speech.
Improper means unsuitable or impolite. The prefix "im-" here does not mean wrong; impromptu means done without preparation.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The manager of the team is often "maligned" by the supporters.

options.why: To malign someone is to speak falsely and spitefully about them, which matches slandered.
Cherished means loved and valued, the opposite of maligned.
options.whyWrong: Cherished is positive, while maligned means spoken badly about.

options.why: Praised is the opposite of maligned.
options.whyWrong: To malign is to attack with harsh or unfair words, not praise.

options.why: Hounded means chased or harassed persistently, not specifically spoken against.
options.whyWrong: Hounded means pursued or harassed, whereas maligned specifically means spoken ill of or slandered.

questions.hint: Remember the root "mal-" means bad or evil (as in malice).
questions.explanation: To "malign" someone means to say harmful, unfair or false things about them in public. "Slandered" means making false spoken statements that damage a person's reputation.
questions.trap: Option D (hounded) is negative too, so students confuse them. Maligned is about bad speech (slander), while hounded is about chasing or pestering.
questions.mnemonic: Mal = bad; maligned = spoken badly about (slandered).

askPresets.answer: When fans spread unfair rumours about a coach after a loss, they malign (slander) him.
Hounded means constantly chased or harassed, whereas maligned specifically refers to speaking evil or false things about someone.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the phrase in quotes: He has "a cogent" reason for quitting the relationship.

options.why: Cogent means clear, logical and convincing.
Important means significant, whereas cogent specifically means logically persuasive.
options.whyWrong: An important reason matters, but cogent means well-reasoned and convincing.

options.why: Tentative means uncertain or hesitant, the opposite of cogent.
options.whyWrong: Tentative means unsure and subject to change, whereas a cogent reason is strong and clear.

options.why: Unacceptable is negative and does not match cogent.
options.whyWrong: A cogent reason is strong and believable, not unacceptable.

questions.hint: Think of a reason that forces you to agree because the logic is strong.
questions.explanation: A "cogent" argument or reason is one that is clear, logical and persuasive, so "a convincing" reason is nearest in meaning.
questions.trap: Option B (an important) seems close, but "cogent" highlights logical force and persuasiveness rather than mere importance.

askPresets.answer: If your friend gives clear facts that make everyone agree with her choice, her reason is cogent.
An important reason has weight, while a cogent reason is specifically clear, logical and convincing.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the phrase in quotes: Mrs. Adio wasn't yet "attuned to" her baby's needs.

options.why: To be attuned to something means to be used to and sensitive to it, matching familiar with.
Ready with means having something prepared to hand over, not understanding needs.
options.whyWrong: Ready with does not express being accustomed to or understanding someone's needs.

options.why: Free from means not having or affected by something, which reverses the sense.
options.whyWrong: Free from means without; a mother is learning to respond to her baby's needs, not avoiding them.

options.why: Planning for means preparing ahead, not being used to or in tune with.
options.whyWrong: Planning for looks ahead, whereas attuned to means already used to and understanding.

questions.hint: Think of "in tune with" — when you know how something works or sounds.
questions.explanation: To be "attuned to" someone's needs means to have grown used to them and able to understand and respond well, so "familiar with" fits best.
questions.trap: Option D (planning for) sounds plausible in parenting, but "attuned to" is about understanding and familiarity, not making plans.
questions.mnemonic: Attuned to = in tune with = familiar with.

askPresets.answer: A new mother soon becomes attuned to (familiar with) her baby's different cries.
Planning for means making future arrangements, whereas attuned to means having become familiar with and sensitive to something.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: We were at a loss to understand why Oli should "retract" his statement before the Judge.

options.why: Assert means to state firmly, which is the opposite of retract.
options.whyWrong: To assert is to declare firmly, not to take a statement back.

options.why: Repeat means to say again, not to take back.
options.whyWrong: Repeating a statement keeps it standing; retracting pulls it back.

options.why: To retract a statement means to take it back or withdraw it.
Reiterate means to say again for emphasis, the opposite of retract.
options.whyWrong: Reiterate means repeat, whereas retract means take back.

questions.hint: Think of the root "re-" (back) + "tract" (pull, as in tractor): pull back.
questions.explanation: "Retract" means to pull back or take back something you said or promised. In court, taking back a statement means to withdraw it.
questions.trap: Options B (repeat) and D (reiterate) both start with "re-", tempting students who misread "retract" as saying again rather than pulling back.

askPresets.answer: When a witness tells the judge, "I take back what I said earlier," she retracts (withdraws) her statement.
Assert means to state something confidently as true, which is the opposite of retracting (taking back) a statement.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The workers hope to appear before the "arbitration" panel to resolve the lingering dispute.

options.why: A trial panel judges crimes or lawsuits in court, rather than settling workplace disputes by agreement.
options.whyWrong: A trial is a formal court hearing to decide guilt or liability, whereas arbitration settles disputes out of court.

options.why: Legislative relates to making laws, not settling disputes.
options.whyWrong: Legislative means law-making, which is not the role of a dispute panel.

options.why: Investigative means looking into facts, not settling a dispute between sides.
options.whyWrong: An investigative panel only uncovers facts; an arbitration panel helps settle the disagreement.

options.why: Arbitration is settling a dispute between opposing sides to bring agreement, closest here to reconciliatory.

questions.hint: Notice the goal in the sentence: "to resolve the lingering dispute".
questions.explanation: "Arbitration" is the process of settling a dispute between two sides through an impartial panel so they reach peace or agreement, which matches "reconciliatory" (aimed at bringing two sides together).
questions.trap: Option A (trial) is tempting because a "panel" sounds legal, but industrial disputes go to arbitration to reconcile sides, not to hold a criminal trial.

askPresets.answer: When a neutral elder helps two neighbours settle a land quarrel peacefully, that is arbitration (reconciliatory).
A trial decides legal guilt or innocence in court, whereas an arbitration panel aims to resolve a dispute and reconcile both sides.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: He was not able to "withstand" the attack from his immediate family.

options.why: Survive means stay alive, whereas withstand means stand firm against.
options.whyWrong: Surviving an attack means living through it, not standing firm against it.

options.why: Overcome means defeat or conquer, which goes further than holding out against.
options.whyWrong: Withstand means resist or hold out against, not defeat the attacker.

options.why: Match means equal in strength, not hold out against.
options.whyWrong: To match an attack is to equal it; to withstand is to resist it.

options.why: Withstand means stand firm against or resist.

questions.hint: Break the word apart: with- (against) + stand = stand firm against.
questions.explanation: "Withstand" means to stand firm against pressure or an attack without giving way, which means to resist.
questions.trap: Option B (overcome) means defeating the attack completely, which is stronger than simply resisting or standing firm against it.

askPresets.answer: Strong pillars withstand (resist) heavy winds without collapsing.
Overcome means to conquer or defeat something, while withstand simply means to hold out and resist without giving in.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Your effort to bring peace between us is futile because you are "biased".

options.why: Convinced means certain of something, not unfairly favouring one side.
options.whyWrong: Being convinced means sure of a fact, whereas biased means unfairly taking sides.

options.why: Clever means intelligent, unrelated to taking sides.
options.whyWrong: Cleverness has nothing to do with unfair favouritism.

options.why: Biased means unfairly favouring or disliking one side, which matches prejudiced.
Worried means anxious, not unfair.
options.whyWrong: Being worried does not stop someone from judging fairly.

questions.hint: Why would a peacemaker fail? Because they already favour one side.
questions.explanation: To be "biased" means to have an unfair preference for or against one side rather than judging neutrally. "Prejudiced" means having that same unfair pre-judgement.
questions.trap: Option A (convinced) means persuaded of something, but a biased person has formed an unfair opinion without weighing both sides.

askPresets.answer: If a referee always favours his home team, he is biased (prejudiced).
Convinced means persuaded by reasons or evidence, whereas biased means unfairly leaning toward one side.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the phrase in quotes: His embroidery was "an exacting" task for the tailor.

options.why: Unwarranted means unjustified or uncalled for, not difficult.
options.whyWrong: Unwarranted means without good reason, whereas exacting describes how much care and effort a task demands.

options.why: Exciting means thrilling, which looks similar to exacting but has a different meaning.
options.whyWrong: Exciting means thrilling, whereas exacting means demanding great care and effort.

options.why: Exacting means requiring great skill, care and effort, which matches demanding.
Disturbing means upsetting or worrying, not requiring skill and patience.
options.whyWrong: Disturbing means causing worry, whereas an exacting task demands strict attention.

questions.hint: Do not confuse "exacting" with "exciting" — think of needing to be exact.
questions.explanation: An "exacting" task is one that requires great precision, time and effort, so "a demanding" task is nearest in meaning.
questions.trap: Option B (an exciting) is a look-alike trap for "exacting". Careful embroidery demands patience and precision, not excitement.

askPresets.answer: Watch-repairing is an exacting (demanding) job because one tiny slip spoils the watch.
Exciting looks almost the same in spelling, but exacting means demanding high precision and effort, not thrilling.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Nobody knew the source of the "altercation" between the couple.

options.why: An alter ego is a second self or very close friend, not a quarrel.
options.whyWrong: Alter ego sounds like altercation because of 'alter', but it means another side of someone's personality.

options.why: An altercation is a noisy argument or quarrel.
Deep love is the opposite of a heated quarrel.
options.whyWrong: Altercation means a heated argument, not affection.

options.why: Conservative is an adjective meaning traditional or cautious, unrelated to a quarrel.
options.whyWrong: Conservative does not fit grammatically or in meaning after 'source of the'.

questions.hint: Ignore the look-alike "alter ego" and ask what happens between a couple that has a "source".
questions.explanation: An "altercation" is a heated or noisy argument between people, so "quarrel" is nearest in meaning.
questions.trap: Option A (alter ego) shares the root "alter", tricking students who guess from spelling rather than meaning.

askPresets.answer: Two drivers shouting at each other after a minor bump are having an altercation (quarrel).
An alter ego is a trusted close friend or a person's second personality, whereas an altercation is a loud quarrel.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: I had to make my way through the "throng" of people in the church.

options.why: A group can be just a few people, smaller than a dense throng.
options.whyWrong: A group may be small and orderly, whereas a throng is a large, tightly packed crowd.

options.why: A throng is a large, densely packed crowd of people.
A gathering is any meeting of people, not necessarily packed tightly together.
options.whyWrong: A gathering does not suggest squeezing through a packed mass the way throng and crowd do.

options.why: Theme means topic or subject, unrelated to people.
options.whyWrong: Theme means a central idea, not a mass of people.

questions.hint: Clue: "make my way through" suggests squeezing past many tightly packed people.
questions.explanation: A "throng" is a large, tightly packed mass of people in one place, so "crowd" is nearest in meaning.
questions.trap: Option C (gathering) describes people meeting, while "crowd" captures the dense mass you have to push or make your way through.

askPresets.answer: At a busy market or stadium gate, you push through a throng (crowd) of people.
A gathering is any meeting of people, whereas a throng specifically means a dense crowd you have to squeeze through.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The man's wife has her "misgivings" about him.

options.why: Fears for means worrying about someone's safety, not doubting their character.
options.whyWrong: Fearing for someone means worrying about their wellbeing, whereas misgivings means doubts or distrust.

options.why: Misgivings are feelings of doubt, worry or suspicion, matching distrust of.
Hatred is intense dislike, stronger and different from doubt.
options.whyWrong: Hatred means loathing someone, while misgivings means feeling uneasy doubts or distrust.

options.why: Love is positive, the opposite of misgivings.
options.whyWrong: Misgivings are uneasy doubts, not affection.

questions.hint: Notice "mis-givings" = bad feelings or doubts about someone's honesty or motives.
questions.explanation: "Misgivings" are feelings of doubt, suspicion or apprehension about someone or something. Having misgivings about someone means having distrust of them.
questions.trap: Option A (fears for) means being afraid that something bad will happen to him, not doubting or distrusting him.

askPresets.answer: If you lend money to someone who never pays back, you naturally have misgivings (distrust) about lending again.
Fears for means anxiety for a person's safety, whereas misgivings about someone means doubting or distrusting them.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Violent crime is only one of the "maladies" afflicting modern society.

options.why: Damages means harm or money paid for harm, not ailments.
options.whyWrong: Damages refers to physical harm or legal compensation, not diseases or ills.

options.why: A malady is a disease or serious problem (an illness), matching illnesses.
Wounds are physical cuts or injuries, not general ailments.
options.whyWrong: Wounds are injuries to the body, whereas maladies means diseases or deep ills.

options.why: Crises are sudden emergencies or turning points, not ailments.
options.whyWrong: A crisis is an urgent turning point, whereas a malady is a sickness or long-running ill.

questions.hint: Look at the verb "afflicting" and the root "mal-" (bad): sicknesses or ills.
questions.explanation: "Malady" literally means an illness or disease, and figuratively a serious social problem. Among the options, "illnesses" is the direct synonym.
questions.trap: Option D (crises) fits the idea of social trouble, but "maladies" directly translates to "illnesses" (literally or figuratively).

askPresets.answer: Poverty and corruption are often called social maladies (illnesses) that weaken a nation.
Crises are urgent emergencies or turning points, whereas maladies literally means illnesses or ailments.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Everyone was talking about the "camaraderie" in the club.

options.why: Camaraderie means mutual trust and friendly companionship among members of a group.
Quarrelsomeness means arguing often, the opposite of camaraderie.
options.whyWrong: Quarrelsomeness means picking fights, whereas camaraderie is warm friendship.

options.why: Commissioning means officially starting or assigning a task, unrelated to friendship.
options.whyWrong: Commissioning has nothing to do with warm fellowship in a club.

options.why: Disunity means division, the opposite of camaraderie.
options.whyWrong: Disunity means breaking apart, whereas camaraderie binds people together.

questions.hint: Think of "comrade" — a close friend or companion.
questions.explanation: "Camaraderie" comes from the same root as "comrade" and means warm friendship, trust and companionship among people who spend time together.
questions.trap: Option C (commissioning) starts with "c-" and sounds formal, but it means giving authority or launching a project, not friendship.

askPresets.answer: Teammates who joke together and support each other share great camaraderie (companionship).
Commissioning means appointing or launching something officially, not friendly companionship.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The smell is "obnoxious".

options.why: Obnoxious means very unpleasant or disgusting; its opposite is pleasant.
Loathsome means disgusting, which is a synonym of obnoxious.
options.whyWrong: Loathsome means hateful or disgusting, similar to obnoxious rather than opposite.

options.why: Unpleasant is a synonym of obnoxious, not its opposite.
options.whyWrong: Unpleasant means the same as obnoxious; the question asks for the opposite.

options.why: Obvious means easy to see or notice, unrelated to smell quality.
options.whyWrong: Obvious sounds slightly like obnoxious, but it means clear or plain to see.

questions.hint: Notice that both B and C mean the same as obnoxious — cross out synonyms first.
questions.explanation: "Obnoxious" means extremely unpleasant, offensive or disgusting. Its direct opposite is "pleasant".
questions.trap: Option C (unpleasant) is a synonym trap. In antonym questions, rule out every word with the same meaning first.

askPresets.answer: If rotting rubbish has an obnoxious smell, fresh flowers have a pleasant smell.
Unpleasant is a synonym of obnoxious, whereas we need the opposite meaning.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: Aliyu was a natural "spendthrift" when he was single.

options.why: A philanthropist gives money generously to help others, not a hoarder.
options.whyWrong: A philanthropist is generous to charity, whereas the opposite of a wasteful spender is someone who hates spending.

options.why: A spendthrift wastes money carelessly; a miser hoards money and hates spending it.
A gambler risks money on games of chance, which also wastes money.
options.whyWrong: A gambler is reckless with money like a spendthrift, not the opposite.

options.why: Thrift collector is a distractor made up from the word 'thrift'.
options.whyWrong: A thrift collector collects savings for people, not the opposite personality to a spendthrift.

questions.hint: Warning: despite the word "thrift" inside it, a spendthrift SPENDS away thrift (savings) recklessly!
questions.explanation: A "spendthrift" is someone who spends money extravagantly and wastefully. The opposite is a "miser", someone who hoards wealth and refuses to spend.
questions.trap: Option D (thrift collector) catches students who see "thrift" inside "spendthrift" and guess a thrift-related job.
questions.mnemonic: Spendthrift = wastes money <-> miser = hoards money.

askPresets.answer: A spendthrift buys everything on impulse; a miser counts every kobo and locks it away.
Thrift collector is a trap built around the word 'thrift'; a spendthrift wastes money, so its opposite is a miser.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The decision will have no "adverse" effect on us.

options.why: Inimical means harmful or hostile, which is a synonym of adverse.
options.whyWrong: Inimical means harmful or unfriendly, the same direction as adverse.

options.why: Detrimental means damaging, a synonym of adverse.
options.whyWrong: Detrimental means harmful, which is a synonym rather than an opposite.

options.why: Adverse means harmful or unfavourable; its opposite is beneficial.
Lasting means enduring for a long time, unrelated to good or bad effect.
options.whyWrong: Lasting tells how long an effect stays, not whether it is good or harmful.

questions.hint: Both A and B mean harmful — so the opposite must mean helpful.
questions.explanation: "Adverse" means harmful, unfavourable or working against you. Its opposite is "beneficial" (helpful or bringing good results).
questions.trap: Option B (detrimental) is a synonym of adverse, catching students who forget the question asks for the opposite.

askPresets.answer: Heavy flooding has an adverse (harmful) effect on crops, while gentle rain has a beneficial effect.
Detrimental means harmful or damaging, which is a synonym of adverse, not its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: I "despise" the way she lived her life.

options.why: Abhor means to hate strongly, a synonym of despise.
options.whyWrong: Abhor means hate or detest, which means the same as despise.

options.why: Hate is a synonym of despise.
options.whyWrong: Hate means almost the same as despise, not the opposite.

options.why: To despise is to look down on with contempt; its opposite is admire.
Remember means recall to mind, not respect or love.
options.whyWrong: Remembering does not show approval or disapproval.

questions.hint: Rule out the two words that mean strong dislike (abhor and hate).
questions.explanation: To "despise" means to feel strong contempt or scorn for someone or something. Its opposite is to "admire" (regard with respect and approval).
questions.trap: Option A (abhor) is a high-level synonym of despise. Always check whether the instruction asks for nearest or opposite in meaning.

askPresets.answer: You despise dishonest tricks, but you admire hard work and honesty.
Abhor means to hate or detest, which is a synonym of despise rather than its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: I am happy to inform you that your boys are "conscientious".

options.why: Industrious means hardworking, which goes with conscientious rather than against it.
options.whyWrong: Industrious is a positive trait like conscientious, not its opposite.

options.why: Conscientious means careful, thorough and dutiful; carefree means untroubled and casual about duties.
Careful is close in meaning to conscientious.
options.whyWrong: Careful is similar to conscientious, not opposite.

options.why: Corrupt means dishonest, whereas conscientious focuses on carefulness and diligence.
options.whyWrong: Corrupt means taking bribes or acting dishonestly, whereas carefree directly contrasts with careful, dutiful effort.

questions.hint: Think of the root "conscience" + care: someone who works carefully and dutifully.
questions.explanation: "Conscientious" means taking great care to do one's work properly and dutifully. Its opposite here is "carefree" (casual, unconcerned and not taking duties seriously).
questions.trap: Option D (corrupt) is negative, so students pick it quickly, but "conscientious" means careful and diligent (opposite: carefree), not simply "honest".

askPresets.answer: A conscientious student checks every answer; a carefree student rushes without caring.
Corrupt means dishonest or bribable, whereas conscientious means diligent and careful, whose opposite here is carefree.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The man who had been seriously ill was "convalescing" at a seaside resort.

options.why: Regaining health is the definition of convalescing, a synonym.
options.whyWrong: Regaining health means the exact same thing as convalescing.

options.why: Convalescing means recovering from illness; deteriorating in health is the opposite.
Recuperating means recovering, a synonym of convalescing.
options.whyWrong: Recuperating is a synonym of convalescing, not its opposite.

options.why: Relaxing means resting, which often goes with recovering.
options.whyWrong: Relaxing does not oppose recovering from an illness.

questions.hint: Both A and C mean getting better after sickness — we want the opposite.
questions.explanation: "Convalescing" means gradually recovering health and strength after an illness or operation. Its opposite is "deteriorating in health" (getting worse).
questions.trap: Option C (recuperating) is a close synonym of convalescing, tempting students who forget the instruction asks for the opposite.
questions.mnemonic: Convalescing = getting better <-> deteriorating = getting worse.

askPresets.answer: A patient who is convalescing is getting stronger day by day; the opposite is deteriorating in health.
Recuperating means recovering from an illness, which is a synonym of convalescing, not the opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: For millions of years, the world's resources have remained "boundless".

options.why: Unlimited is a synonym of boundless.
options.whyWrong: Unlimited means having no limit, the same as boundless.

options.why: Scarce means rare or in short supply, whereas boundless is directly about having no bounds or limits.
options.whyWrong: Scarce means hard to find, whereas boundless literally means without limits; its direct opposite is limited.

options.why: Indomitable means impossible to defeat, unrelated to limits.
options.whyWrong: Indomitable means unconquerable, not limited.

options.why: Boundless means having no boundaries or limits; its exact opposite is limited.

questions.hint: Look at the suffix "-less" (without bounds) -> the exact opposite has a bound or limit.
questions.explanation: "Boundless" means without limit or end. Its exact opposite is "limited" (restricted in amount or extent).
questions.trap: Option B (scarce) is tempting because both "scarce" and "limited" suggest not having enough, but "limited" is the exact antonym of "boundless" (unlimited).

askPresets.answer: If the sky seems boundless (without limit), a small tank of fuel is limited.
Scarce means rare or insufficient, while limited directly opposes boundless (without limits).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The difference between the experimental procedures was "imperceptible" to me.

options.why: Negligible means too small to matter, close in sense to imperceptible.
options.whyWrong: Negligible means tiny or unimportant, similar to imperceptible rather than opposite.

options.why: Significant means important or meaningful, rather than easily seen or noticed.
options.whyWrong: Significant means important, whereas imperceptible means impossible to perceive; its direct opposite is obvious.

options.why: Imperceptible means too slight to be seen or noticed; its opposite is obvious.
Obscure means unclear or hidden, close in sense to imperceptible.
options.whyWrong: Obscure means hard to see or understand, similar to imperceptible.

questions.hint: "Im-perceptible" = cannot be perceived (seen or noticed). What is easy to notice?
questions.explanation: "Imperceptible" means so small or gradual that it cannot be seen or noticed. Its opposite is "obvious" (easily seen or clear).
questions.trap: Option B (significant) is tempting in science sentences, but "imperceptible" is about visibility/noticeability (opposite: obvious), not importance.
questions.mnemonic: Imperceptible = hard to notice <-> obvious = easy to see.

askPresets.answer: A tiny hairline crack may be imperceptible, while a wide gap is obvious.
Significant means important or sizable, whereas imperceptible refers to whether something can be noticed at all (opposite: obvious).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The officer said that he knew nothing to the "detriment" of the applicant.

options.why: Damage is close in meaning to detriment.
options.whyWrong: Damage means harm, which is similar to detriment rather than opposite.

options.why: Disfavour means disapproval, on the same negative side as detriment.
options.whyWrong: Disfavour is negative like detriment, not its opposite.

options.why: Detriment means harm or disadvantage; its opposite is advantage.
Background refers to past history, not harm or benefit.
options.whyWrong: Background is neutral and does not oppose detriment.

questions.hint: "To the detriment of" means to the harm or disadvantage of someone.
questions.explanation: "Detriment" means harm, damage or disadvantage. Its opposite is "advantage" (something helpful or in one's favour).
questions.trap: Option B (disfavour) sounds formal and negative, tempting students who forget to reverse the meaning.

askPresets.answer: Staying up all night before an exam works to your detriment; sleeping well works to your advantage.
Disfavour means disapproval or disadvantage, which is close to detriment rather than its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: Common sense requires that one should be "decorous" at formal gatherings.

options.why: Courteous means polite, a synonym of decorous.
options.whyWrong: Courteous means polite and well-behaved, the same as decorous.

options.why: Decorous means polite, dignified and well-behaved; its opposite is impolite.
Incurious means not curious or uninterested, unrelated to good manners.
options.whyWrong: Incurious means showing no curiosity, not bad manners.

options.why: Careful means cautious, which goes with decorous rather than opposing it.
options.whyWrong: Careful does not oppose polite, proper behaviour.

questions.hint: Connect "decorous" with "decorum" (good, polite behaviour at formal events).
questions.explanation: "Decorous" means polite, proper and well-mannered in keeping with good taste. Its opposite is "impolite" (rude or ill-mannered).
questions.trap: Option A (courteous) is a synonym of decorous. Check the instruction carefully so you do not pick the synonym.

askPresets.answer: At a wedding or graduation ceremony, guests are expected to be decorous (polite), not impolite.
Courteous means polite and respectful, which is a synonym of decorous, not the opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The string was "taut".

options.why: Taut means pulled tight with no slack; its opposite is loose.
Firm is close in meaning to taut.
options.whyWrong: Firm means stiff or tight, similar to taut.

options.why: Stretched describes a tight string, a synonym of taut.
options.whyWrong: A stretched string is tight (taut), not the opposite.

options.why: Tight is a direct synonym of taut.
options.whyWrong: Tight means the same as taut; the question asks for the opposite.

questions.hint: Notice that B, C and D all describe a pulled string — only one option leaves slack.
questions.explanation: "Taut" means stretched or pulled tight so there is no slack. Its opposite is "loose" (slack, not pulled tight).
questions.trap: Options B (firm), C (stretched) and D (tight) all mean nearly the same thing as taut. Crossing out synonyms leaves A.

askPresets.answer: Pull a washing line until it is taut (tight); untie one end and it becomes loose.
Stretched means pulled tight, which is what taut means, not its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The teacher announced that the class would be making a "fleeting" visit to the zoo.

options.why: Routine means regular or habitual, not contrasting with short duration.
options.whyWrong: Routine means done regularly as a habit, whereas fleeting specifically means brief or short-lived.

options.why: Brief is a synonym of fleeting.
options.whyWrong: Brief means short in time, the same as fleeting.

options.why: Fleeting means lasting a very short time; its opposite is long.
Guided means led by a guide, unrelated to how long the visit lasts.
options.whyWrong: Guided describes who leads the visit, not its length.

questions.hint: A "fleeting" visit flies past quickly — what kind of visit takes plenty of time?
questions.explanation: "Fleeting" means lasting for only a very short time. Its opposite is "long".
questions.trap: Option B (brief) is the direct synonym of fleeting. Always double-check whether the prompt says nearest or opposite.

askPresets.answer: A fleeting glance lasts one second; a long visit lasts hours.
Brief means short, which is a synonym of fleeting rather than its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The project is designed to "alleviate" poverty in the country.

options.why: Tackle means deal with or work to solve a problem, similar in aim to alleviate.
options.whyWrong: Tackling poverty means trying to reduce it, not making it worse.

options.why: Alleviate means make pain or a problem less severe; exacerbate means make it worse.
Eradicate means wipe out completely, which is on the same helping side as alleviate.
options.whyWrong: Eradicating poverty removes it altogether, whereas the opposite of reducing a problem is making it worse.

options.why: Assuage means calm or lessen, a synonym of alleviate.
options.whyWrong: Assuage means ease or lessen, similar to alleviate.

questions.hint: Look for the word that makes a bad situation worse rather than better.
questions.explanation: To "alleviate" means to make suffering or a problem less severe. Its opposite is "exacerbate" (to make a bad situation worse).
questions.trap: Option C (eradicate) is tempting because it differs in degree, yet both alleviate and eradicate fight poverty, whereas exacerbate worsens it.

askPresets.answer: Medicine alleviates (eases) a headache; loud noise exacerbates (worsens) it.
Eradicate means completely destroy a problem, which goes in the same direction as alleviate rather than opposing it.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: As these boys never act in public, the police are now worried about their "covert" activities.

options.why: Cryptic means mysterious or coded, similar to covert.
options.whyWrong: Cryptic means hidden or puzzling, similar to covert rather than opposite.

options.why: Ignoble means dishonourable, unrelated to secret vs public.
options.whyWrong: Ignoble means shameful, not open or public.

options.why: Evil means wicked, unrelated to whether an act is hidden or open.
options.whyWrong: Covert tells us the acts are hidden, not whether they are good or evil.

options.why: Covert means hidden or secret; its opposite is open.

questions.hint: Clue in the sentence: "never act in public" tells you what "covert" means.
questions.explanation: "Covert" means secret or hidden (think of "covered"). Its opposite is "open" (done plainly in public).
questions.trap: Option A (cryptic) sounds learned and means hidden/mysterious, which is a synonym of covert, not the opposite.

askPresets.answer: Covert meetings happen behind closed doors; open meetings happen in full view.
Cryptic means mysterious or concealed, which is close to covert rather than its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the phrase in quotes: Updating the Board's brochure is "an arduous" task.

options.why: Annual means yearly, unrelated to difficulty.
options.whyWrong: Annual describes how often a task happens, not how hard it is.

options.why: Arduous means hard and tiring; its opposite is easy.
Regular means happening at set intervals, unrelated to effort.
options.whyWrong: Regular is about timing, not ease or difficulty.

options.why: Difficult is a direct synonym of arduous.
options.whyWrong: Difficult means the same as arduous, not its opposite.

questions.hint: Notice D (difficult) is the synonym, so the opposite must be B.
questions.explanation: "Arduous" means very difficult and requiring hard, tiring effort. Its opposite is "an easy" task.
questions.trap: Option D (a difficult) is the exact synonym of arduous. Check whether the question asks for nearest or opposite in meaning.

askPresets.answer: Climbing a steep mountain is arduous; walking on flat ground is easy.
Difficult means hard to do, which is a synonym of arduous rather than its opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the interpretation that you consider appropriate for the sentence: When asked to state her side of the story, Bunmi started by beating about the bush.

options.text: She went straight to the point.
options.why: Going straight to the point is the opposite of beating about the bush.
options.whyWrong: Beating about the bush means avoiding the main point, not going straight to it.

options.text: She was lost in great thought.
options.why: Being lost in thought means daydreaming or thinking deeply, not avoiding the main topic.
options.whyWrong: The idiom describes how someone speaks around an issue, not quiet daydreaming.

options.why: This takes 'bush' literally.
options.whyWrong: Idioms are figurative; she was speaking indirectly, not walking through a bush.

options.text: She approached the subject without coming to the point.
options.why: Beating about the bush means talking around an issue without stating the main point directly.

questions.hint: Never read an idiom word for word — nobody is walking in a bush here.
questions.explanation: "To beat about the bush" means to talk around a topic or delay saying what you really mean instead of coming straight to the point.
questions.trap: Option C takes the word "bush" literally as a physical bush path. Idioms carry figurative meaning, not literal scenery.
questions.mnemonic: Beat about the bush = circle around the point.

askPresets.answer: If you broke a plate and start talking about the weather before mentioning the plate, you are beating about the bush.
Following a bush path reads 'bush' literally; the idiom means talking indirectly without getting to the point.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the interpretation that you consider appropriate for the sentence: The amount he donated was small. He said it was his widow's mite.

options.why: A widow is a woman whose husband has died, and the phrase is figurative.
options.whyWrong: A man cannot be a widow; the phrase describes a small gift from someone with little money.

options.why: Miserly means stingy, whereas a widow's mite is generous relative to what the giver has.
options.whyWrong: Someone giving their widow's mite is giving generously from small means, not being stingy.

options.text: It was all he could honestly afford.
options.why: A widow's mite is a small contribution that represents the best a person of modest means can give.
Saying it is a widow's mite implies the giver could not easily afford more.
options.whyWrong: The idiom means the small amount was a sincere stretch for the giver, not that he held back.

questions.hint: This expression comes from the biblical story of a poor widow who gave two tiny coins — all she had.
questions.explanation: "A widow's mite" means a small donation that is genuinely all the giver can afford, given willingly despite limited means.
questions.trap: Option D reverses the sense: a person offering a widow's mite is not holding back wealth, they are giving what little they can.
questions.mnemonic: Widow's mite = small gift, all one can afford.

askPresets.answer: A student donating ₦200 out of her ₦500 pocket money is giving her widow's mite.
Saying he could have given more ignores the origin of the idiom, which honours a small gift from someone who has very little.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the interpretation that you consider appropriate for the sentence: The friendship between Segun and Shehu has turned sour.

options.text: Segun and Shehu are no longer friends.
options.why: When a relationship turns sour, it spoils and ends in bad feeling.

options.text: Segun and Shehu are still friends.
options.why: Turning sour means the friendship has gone bad.
options.whyWrong: Milk that turns sour is spoilt; a friendship that turns sour is broken, not still warm.

options.text: Segun and Shehu are better friends now.
options.why: Better friends is the opposite of turning sour.
options.whyWrong: Sour carries a negative, spoilt sense, not improvement.

options.text: Segun and Shehu are getting to understand each other.
options.why: Understanding each other builds friendship, whereas turning sour means falling out.
options.whyWrong: Turning sour means the friendship has gone bad and ended.

questions.hint: Think of fresh milk that "turns sour" — it goes bad and can no longer be enjoyed.
questions.explanation: When a friendship or partnership "turns sour", goodwill turns into bitterness or hostility, so the two people are no longer friends.
questions.trap: Option D suggests growing closer, forgetting that "sour" always means spoilt or bitter in this idiom.
questions.mnemonic: Turned sour = went bad = no longer friends.

askPresets.answer: Two close classmates who stop speaking after a quarrel have seen their friendship turn sour.
Fresh milk that turns sour is spoilt; likewise, a friendship that turns sour has broken down.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the interpretation that you consider appropriate for the sentence: The driver smelled a rat when the policemen asked him to stop.

options.why: Reckless means careless, not sensing danger or trickery.
options.whyWrong: Being reckless means driving without care, whereas smelling a rat means suspecting a trick or trouble.

options.why: To smell a rat means to suspect that something is wrong or dishonest.
Careful means cautious, which misses the idea of suspecting something hidden.
options.whyWrong: While suspicion may make someone cautious, smelling a rat specifically means becoming suspicious.

options.why: Offensive means rude or insulting, unrelated to sensing trouble.
options.whyWrong: Smelling a rat is about suspicion inside one's mind, not rude behaviour.

questions.hint: Ask yourself what you feel when you suspect someone is setting a trap or hiding something.
questions.explanation: "To smell a rat" means to suspect that something wrong, dishonest or deceptive is going on, so the driver became suspicious.
questions.trap: Option C (careful) is close to how a suspicious driver might act, but the exact meaning of the idiom is feeling suspicion.
questions.mnemonic: Smell a rat = suspect a trick = suspicious.

askPresets.answer: If a stranger offers to double your money in five minutes, you should smell a rat (be suspicious).
Being careful means acting cautiously in general, whereas smelling a rat specifically means suspecting trickery or trouble.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the interpretation that you consider appropriate for the sentence: From the way Ngozi behaves, it is obvious she is a greenhorn.

options.why: Arrogant means proud, whereas greenhorn means new and inexperienced.
options.whyWrong: Being a greenhorn is about lack of experience, not pride.

options.why: Cautious means careful, not inexperienced.
options.whyWrong: Cautious describes care, whereas greenhorn describes a beginner.

options.why: A greenhorn is a beginner or someone new to a job or place who lacks experience.
Uncivilised means lacking manners or culture, not lacking experience.
options.whyWrong: Greenhorn means a newcomer without experience, not someone rude.

questions.hint: Think of a young "green" shoot or "green" fruit that is not yet ripe or seasoned.
questions.explanation: A "greenhorn" (like "green" for unripe) is a beginner who lacks experience and still has much to learn.
questions.trap: Option B (cautious) or D (uncivilised) are common guesses when students do not know "green" means fresh and inexperienced.

askPresets.answer: A brand-new apprentice on her first day at a workshop is a greenhorn (inexperienced).
Cautious means careful, whereas a greenhorn specifically means someone who is new and inexperienced.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Kunle was allowed to stew in his own juice.

options.text: He enjoyed the fruits of his labour.
options.why: Enjoying rewards is positive, whereas stewing in your own juice is unpleasant.
options.whyWrong: This idiom refers to facing trouble you caused yourself, not enjoying rewards.

options.text: He suffered the consequences of his action.
options.why: To stew in one's own juice means to be left alone to suffer the bad results of one's own foolish behaviour.

options.text: He associated with the rich in the society.
options.why: Being rich has nothing to do with this idiom.
options.whyWrong: Stewing in your own juice means facing trouble alone, not mixing with rich people.

options.why: Untold hardship leaves out the key point that Kunle brought the trouble on himself.
options.whyWrong: The idiom specifically means suffering the results of your own actions without anyone rescuing you.

questions.hint: Notice the phrase "in his OWN juice" — he caused the mess himself and was left to deal with it.
questions.explanation: To let someone "stew in their own juice" means to leave them to face the unpleasant consequences of their own actions without stepping in to rescue them.
questions.trap: Option D (untold hardship) sounds close, but it misses the essential meaning of "own juice": suffering the results of one's own action.
questions.mnemonic: Stew in his own juice = face his own mess.

askPresets.answer: If a student refuses to study despite warnings and then has to repeat the test alone, he is stewing in his own juice.
Untold hardship is too broad and misses the key idea that he brought the trouble upon himself.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The team's poor performance at the tournament plumbed the depths of horror.

options.why: Rewards follow success, not a dreadful performance.
options.whyWrong: Plumbing the depths of horror describes an awful failure, not a rewarded show.

options.text: The team's performance took them to the next round.
options.why: Advancing would mean success, the opposite of poor performance.
options.whyWrong: The sentence explicitly calls their performance poor and horrifying.

options.text: The team's performance was enjoyed by all.
options.why: Enjoyment contradicts both 'poor' and 'horror'.
options.whyWrong: Nobody enjoys a performance described as plumbing the depths of horror.

options.text: The team's performance was full of disappointment.
options.why: To plumb the depths of something bad means to reach the very lowest, worst point of it.

questions.hint: Look at the clues "poor performance" and "horror" — the meaning must be strongly negative.
questions.explanation: "To plumb the depths" means to reach the lowest possible level. Plumbing the depths of horror means the team played so badly that their display was deeply disappointing and shocking.
questions.trap: The other three options are all positive, which clashes directly with "poor performance" and "horror".
questions.mnemonic: Plumb the depths = hit rock bottom.

askPresets.answer: If a football team loses 8–0 with three own goals, their display plumbs the depths (is full of disappointment).
A poor performance that reaches the depths of horror cannot be rewarded; it was deeply disappointing.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the underlined expression: The government should stop "white elephant projects".

options.text: projects in which white men kill elephants
options.why: This reads 'white' and 'elephant' literally.
options.whyWrong: White elephant is a fixed idiom; it has nothing to do with hunting elephants.

options.text: projects in which white elephants are used
options.why: This takes the words literally.
options.whyWrong: No real elephants are used; a white elephant is something expensive and useless.

options.text: projects for painting some elephants white
options.why: This reads the phrase literally as painting animals.
options.whyWrong: Idioms are figurative; white elephant means costly to maintain yet useless.

options.text: high cost projects with low utility values
options.why: A white elephant is a costly scheme or possession that brings little or no practical benefit.

questions.hint: Ignore any option that mentions real elephants or painting.
questions.explanation: A "white elephant" is something expensive to build and maintain that gives little or no useful return. So "white elephant projects" are costly projects of very low practical value.
questions.trap: Options A, B and C all read "white" and "elephant" literally. Whenever an option repeats the literal animals or objects of an idiom, reject it.
questions.mnemonic: White elephant = costly to keep, little use.

askPresets.answer: A giant multi-billion-naira airport built in a town where no planes ever land is a white elephant project.
Options mentioning real elephants take the idiom word for word; figuratively it means expensive projects with very low usefulness.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the underlined expression: His attempts were "nipped in the bud".

options.why: Unsuccessful gives the result loosely, without capturing that they were stopped right at the start.
options.whyWrong: While being nipped in the bud leads to failure, the exact meaning is being cut short early before growing.

options.why: To nip something in the bud means to stop or cut it short at an early stage before it develops.
Frustrated is about emotion or blocking, less exact than cutting something short early.
options.whyWrong: Nipped in the bud specifically stresses stopping a plan early, like pinching a flower bud before it opens.

options.why: Disqualified means ruled out of a contest, too narrow for this idiom.
options.whyWrong: Disqualified applies to rules in competitions, whereas nipping in the bud means stopping anything at the very start.

questions.hint: Picture pinching off a flower bud before it even opens into a blossom.
questions.explanation: "To nip in the bud" comes from gardening: pinching off a bud before it blooms. It means to stop a plan or trouble early — to cut it short before it grows.
questions.trap: Option A (unsuccessful) is close in outcome, but "cut short" captures the exact image of stopping something early.
questions.mnemonic: Nip in the bud = cut short early.

askPresets.answer: Security officers caught the plotters on day one, so the coup was nipped in the bud (cut short).
Unsuccessful only says it failed, whereas nipped in the bud specifically means stopped early or cut short before it could grow.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the underlined expression: The account clerk was jailed because he "cooked the books".

options.text: set fire to the account books
options.why: This takes 'cooked' literally as burning.
options.whyWrong: Cooking the books is figurative; it means falsifying financial records, not burning them.

options.text: sold the books in his office to get money for good
options.why: This takes 'books' literally as objects to sell.
options.whyWrong: Account books are financial ledgers; cooking them means faking the figures.

options.text: falsified the accounts to his advantage
options.why: To cook the books means to alter financial records dishonestly to hide theft or show false figures.

options.text: destroyed the accounts books by cooking them
options.why: This reads 'cooked' literally as boiling or roasting.
options.whyWrong: You cannot eat account ledgers; cooking the books means changing numbers dishonestly.

questions.hint: An account clerk deals with financial ledgers ('the books') — what crime puts an accountant in jail?
questions.explanation: "To cook the books" is an idiom meaning to tamper with or falsify financial accounts dishonestly, usually to steal money or deceive auditors.
questions.trap: Options A and D read "cooked" literally as heat or food preparation. In accounting, "the books" are financial records, and "cooking" them means faking the numbers.
questions.mnemonic: Cook the books = fake the accounts.

askPresets.answer: Changing a ₦10,000 receipt to ₦100,000 in the office ledger is cooking the books.
Setting fire to account books reads 'cooked' literally; figuratively it means falsifying financial records.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: You live in the city now, ______?

options.why: The main clause uses the ordinary verb 'live', not 'be' (are).
options.whyWrong: There is no 'are' in 'You live in the city now', so the tag needs 'do/don't', not 'are'.

options.why: A positive simple-present statement with 'live' takes the negative auxiliary tag 'don't you'.
'Live ... now' is present tense, whereas 'didn't' is past tense.
options.whyWrong: The word 'now' shows present tense, so past 'didn't' does not agree.

options.why: There is no auxiliary 'have' in 'You live'; use 'don't'.
options.whyWrong: Use 'haven't' only when the main clause has 'have' as its auxiliary (like 'You have lived').

questions.hint: Check two things in question tags: (1) positive statement -> negative tag; (2) no auxiliary verb -> use do/does/did.
questions.explanation: "You live" is positive and in the simple present tense with no auxiliary verb. So we supply the present auxiliary "do" in the negative: "don't you?".
questions.trap: Option C (didn't you) uses the past tense, overlooking the present-tense verb "live" and the time word "now".
questions.mnemonic: Positive present verb (live) -> negative present tag (don't you).

askPresets.answer: "You like rice, don't you?" — no helper verb means use do/don't.
"Didn't you" is past tense, which clashes with the present verb "live" and "now".

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The Flying Eagles of Nigeria couldn't have won the match if they hadn't prepared well, ______?

options.why: 'Couldn't' is negative, so the tag must be positive and keep the same modal 'could'.
options.whyWrong: You cannot use a negative tag after a negative statement ('couldn't'), nor switch 'could' to 'can'.

options.why: A negative statement ('couldn't') requires a positive tag ('could they').
options.whyWrong: Since the main verb is already negative ('couldn't'), repeating 'couldn't' breaks the tag rule.

options.why: The main clause has the negative modal 'couldn't', so the tag must be positive with the same modal: 'could they'.
The tag must match the past modal 'could' used in 'couldn't', not 'can'.
options.whyWrong: The modal in the sentence is 'couldn't', so the tag must keep 'could', not change to 'can'.

questions.hint: Look at the main verb before the comma: "couldn't" is negative, so the tag must be positive and keep "could".
questions.explanation: Question tags repeat the first auxiliary verb of the main clause and flip positive/negative. Since the main clause has "couldn't" (negative), the tag is positive using the same modal: "could they?".
questions.trap: Option B (couldn't they) forgets to flip negative to positive, and D (can they) changes the tense of the modal.

askPresets.answer: "She wouldn't go, would she?" — keep the same helper word and drop the 'not'.
"Couldn't they" keeps the negative in both parts; a negative statement takes a positive tag.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Oloyede always sleeps like a baby, ______?

options.why: A positive statement ('sleeps') needs a negative tag ('doesn't he').
options.whyWrong: Because 'sleeps' is positive, the tag must be negative.

options.why: There is no modal 'could' in the sentence.
options.whyWrong: When there is no modal or auxiliary, supply do/does/did, not 'could'.

options.why: Positive singular present 'sleeps' takes the negative singular present tag 'doesn't he'.
The verb 'sleeps' is simple present (habit), not past, and needs a negative tag.
options.whyWrong: 'Did he' has the wrong tense (past) and the wrong polarity (positive).

questions.hint: Check the subject (Oloyede = he), tense (sleeps = present), and polarity (positive -> negative tag).
questions.explanation: "Oloyede always sleeps" is positive, singular and in the simple present tense. Without an auxiliary verb, we use "does" in the negative to match "sleeps": "doesn't he?".
questions.trap: Option A (does he) picks the right auxiliary and tense, but forgets that a positive statement takes a negative tag.

askPresets.answer: "Ada sings well, doesn't she?"
"Does he" fails to flip the polarity: a positive main clause requires a negative tag ('doesn't he').

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Nkiru has lots of friends, but I have ______.

options.why: 'Little' is used with uncountable nouns (like water), not countable 'friends'.
options.whyWrong: Friends can be counted (one friend, two friends), so you cannot use 'a little'.

options.why: 'Little' is only for uncountable nouns, whereas 'friends' is countable plural.
options.whyWrong: Use 'little' for uncountable things like sugar or time, not countable people like friends.

options.why: 'Only a few' means a small positive number, which softens the sharp contrast with 'lots of friends' compared with bare 'few'.
options.whyWrong: In JAMB contrast sentences with 'but', 'lots of friends' contrasts directly with 'few' (hardly any), whereas 'only a few' focuses on having some.

options.why: 'Friends' is countable plural, and 'but' signals a contrast with 'lots of friends': 'few' means hardly any.

questions.hint: First reject 'little' because 'friends' is countable. Then check the contrast word 'but': lots vs hardly any.
questions.explanation: "Friends" is a countable plural noun, so we must choose between "few" and "only a few" (not "little"). The contrast "lots of friends, but I have..." calls for "few" (meaning very few, almost none).
questions.trap: Option C (only a few) also fits countable nouns, but "few" gives the sharpest direct opposite to "lots of" after "but".
questions.mnemonic: Countable + negative contrast = few (not a few / little).

askPresets.answer: "She has many books, but I have few."
"Only a few" means 'some, though not many', whereas the contrast with 'lots of friends' after 'but' points directly to 'few' (hardly any).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Mrs. Audu wept when she discovered that she had lost her ______ rings.

options.why: Purpose ('wedding') comes immediately before the noun 'rings', after material ('gold').
options.whyWrong: In English adjective order, material ('gold') comes before purpose/type ('wedding').

options.why: Opinion/value ('very expensive') must come before material ('gold') and purpose ('wedding').
options.whyWrong: Adjectives of opinion ('very expensive') always go near the front, before material and purpose.

options.why: Opinion ('very expensive') cannot sit after material ('gold').
options.whyWrong: Place opinion ('very expensive') first, then material ('gold'), then purpose ('wedding').

options.why: Follows standard adjective order: opinion ('very expensive') -> material ('gold') -> purpose ('wedding') + noun ('rings').

questions.hint: Remember OSASCOMP: Opinion comes first, Material ('gold') and Purpose ('wedding') sit closest to the noun.
questions.explanation: English adjectives before a noun follow a fixed order: Opinion ("very expensive") comes first, Material ("gold") comes next, and Purpose/type ("wedding") sits right next to "rings".
questions.trap: Option A puts "wedding" before "gold". Remember that the purpose or category of the noun ("wedding rings") stays glued right next to the noun.
questions.mnemonic: Opinion -> Material -> Purpose + Noun (expensive gold wedding rings).

askPresets.answer: You say 'a lovely leather school bag' (opinion -> material -> purpose), not 'a lovely school leather bag'.
"Very expensive wedding gold rings" puts purpose before material; 'wedding' defines what kind of rings they are, so it sits right before 'rings'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Although he tried hard, the journalist couldn't get ______ information.

options.why: 'Several' is used only with plural countable nouns, never uncountable 'information'.
options.whyWrong: 'Information' is uncountable in English (never 'informations'), so 'several' is wrong.

options.why: You cannot use the indefinite article 'an' before an uncountable noun.
options.whyWrong: Because 'information' cannot be counted as one or two, 'an information' is ungrammatical.

options.why: 'Many' is used only with plural countable nouns.
options.whyWrong: 'Many' pairs with plural countable nouns like 'facts' or 'reports', not uncountable 'information'.

options.why: 'Information' is uncountable, so it takes 'much' in a negative sentence ('couldn't get much information').

questions.hint: Is "information" countable or uncountable in standard English? Can you say "two informations"?
questions.explanation: "Information" is an uncountable noun in standard English — it has no plural and cannot take "an", "many" or "several". With a negative verb ("couldn't get"), "much" is correct.
questions.trap: Option B (an) tempts students who treat "information" as countable (like "a news" or "an advice"). All three — information, advice, equipment — are uncountable.

askPresets.answer: Say 'much information' or 'a piece of information', never 'an information' or 'many informations'.
You cannot put 'an' before uncountable nouns like 'information'; use 'much' or 'a piece of information'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Though Amina was very well paid, ______.

options.text: since she was always short of money
options.why: You cannot pair 'Though' with 'since' to join two clauses.
options.whyWrong: Using 'since' after a 'Though' clause leaves the sentence with no main clause.

options.text: but she was always short of money
options.why: Never use 'but' after a clause beginning with 'Though' or 'Although'.
options.whyWrong: 'Though' already signals the contrast, so adding 'but' is redundant and ungrammatical.

options.text: and when she always short of money
options.why: This has 'and when' plus a missing verb ('was').
options.whyWrong: This option adds an unnecessary conjunction and leaves out the verb 'was'.

options.text: she was always short of money
options.why: A 'Though' clause is a subordinate clause and is followed directly by a main clause with no 'but'.

questions.hint: Rule: "Though / Although ... , [main clause]" — never put "but" in the middle!
questions.explanation: When a sentence starts with "Though" or "Although", that subordinating conjunction already shows contrast. You must follow it straight with the main clause ("she was always short of money"), without adding "but".
questions.trap: Option B ("but she was...") is one of the most common mistakes in Nigerian English. Never combine "although/though" with "but" in the same sentence.

askPresets.answer: Say 'Although it rained, we played', NEVER 'Although it rained, but we played'.
Adding 'but' after a 'Though' clause doubles the contrast conjunction, which is ungrammatical in standard English.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: My teacher asked me ______.

options.why: In reported speech after past 'asked', the present verb 'is' must backshift to 'was'.
options.whyWrong: Because the reporting verb 'asked' is past tense, 'is' should shift to 'was'.

options.why: Uses 'if' + statement word order ('the food was') + past tense backshift ('was') after 'asked'.
Indirect questions use statement word order ('the food was'), not question inversion ('is the food').
options.whyWrong: You cannot keep direct-question word order ('is the food') without quotation marks.

options.why: Uses 'whether' properly, but fails to backshift 'is' to past 'was' after 'asked'.
options.whyWrong: Although 'whether' introduces indirect yes/no questions, past 'asked' requires 'was', not 'is'.

questions.hint: Check two rules for reported questions: (1) statement word order (subject before verb); (2) backshift after past 'asked'.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb ("asked"), two changes happen: question inversion turns into statement order ("the food" before the verb), and present "is" shifts back to past "was".
questions.trap: Option A gets the word order right but forgets to backshift "is" to "was" to match past "asked".

askPresets.answer: Direct: 'Are you ready?' -> Reported: She asked me if I was ready.
In reported questions after 'asked', present-tense 'is' must shift back to past 'was'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Either the teacher or the students ______ to blame.

options.why: 'Students' is plural and stands closer to the verb than 'teacher', so use 'are'.
options.whyWrong: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('students'), which is plural.

options.why: By the rule of proximity, the verb agrees with the closer noun 'students' (plural), so 'are' is right.
'Has being' is ungrammatical in English ('has' takes 'been', and 'students' is plural).
options.whyWrong: Never combine 'has' with 'being', and 'students' requires a plural verb anyway.

options.why: 'Are being to blame' is ungrammatical; the fixed expression is 'be to blame'.
options.whyWrong: We say 'are to blame', not 'are being to blame'.

questions.hint: When "either ... or" joins a singular noun and a plural noun, look at the noun closest to the blank.
questions.explanation: Under the rule of proximity, when "either ... or" or "neither ... nor" joins two subjects, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. Here "students" is nearer and plural, so the verb is "are".
questions.trap: Option A (is) makes the verb agree with the first noun ("the teacher") instead of the nearer noun ("the students").
questions.mnemonic: Either/or: match the verb to the CLOSER noun.

askPresets.answer: 'Either the teacher or the students are...' vs 'Either the students or the teacher is...'
When 'either ... or' joins a singular and a plural subject, the verb matches the closer one ('the students'), so it must be 'are'.

questions.subject: english
questions.concept: a number of vs the number of
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The police claim that a number of stolen cars ______ recovered.

options.why: 'A number of + plural noun' means 'several' and takes a plural verb ('have been').
'The number of' takes singular 'has been', whereas 'a number of' takes plural 'have been'.
options.whyWrong: Do not confuse 'a number of' (meaning several -> plural) with 'the number of' (singular).

options.why: 'Has being' is never grammatical in English; 'has' must be followed by 'been'.
options.whyWrong: The past participle of 'be' is 'been', never 'being', after 'has/have'.

options.why: 'Have being' is ungrammatical; use past participle 'been' after 'have'.
options.whyWrong: After 'have', always use 'been', never 'being'.

questions.hint: Distinguish "A number of" (meaning several -> plural) from "THE number of" (the count -> singular).
questions.explanation: "A number of + plural noun" means "several" or "many", so it takes a plural verb: "have been". (Only "the number of" takes a singular verb.)
questions.trap: Option B (has been) catches students who see the singular word "number" and forget the difference between "a number of" and "the number of".
questions.mnemonic: A number of = plural (have); THE number of = singular (has).

askPresets.answer: 'A number of boys were late' (several boys), vs 'The number of boys is ten' (the total count).
'Has been' is used with 'the number of', whereas 'a number of stolen cars' means several cars and takes plural 'have been'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Each of the houses ______ a new look.

options.why: The subject is 'Each' (singular), so it takes the singular verb 'has'.
'Have' is plural, but 'Each' is always singular.
options.whyWrong: Do not agree with 'houses'; the subject is singular 'Each'.

options.why: 'Were' is plural, which clashes with singular 'Each'.
options.whyWrong: Singular 'Each' requires a singular verb ('was given' or 'has'), not plural 'were'.

options.why: 'Have' is plural and does not agree with singular 'Each'.
options.whyWrong: 'Of the houses' is only a prepositional phrase; the head subject is singular 'Each'.

questions.hint: Cover "of the houses" with your finger: you are left with "Each ______ a new look".
questions.explanation: "Each" is always singular, even when followed by "of the" + a plural noun ("houses"). Ignore "of the houses" and use the singular verb "has".
questions.trap: Option D (have) traps students who make the verb agree with the nearest plural word "houses" instead of the true subject "Each".
questions.mnemonic: Each / Every / One of + plural noun -> SINGULAR verb.

askPresets.answer: 'Each of the boys has a pen', not 'have a pen'.
'Have' agrees with 'houses' instead of the real subject 'Each'. 'Each' is always singular and takes 'has'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Four weeks ______ enough for the police to conclude their investigation.

options.why: 'Four weeks' refers to one complete span of time here, and present 'is' fits the general statement best.
options.whyWrong: Although 'has been' is singular, it shifts to present perfect without a time span like 'already' or 'since'; 'is' states a simple present fact.

options.why: A length of time ('Four weeks') measured as a single period takes a singular verb, not 'are'.
options.whyWrong: We treat four weeks as one unit of time, so plural 'are' is wrong.

options.why: Plural 'were' treats the four weeks as separate items instead of one single period.
options.whyWrong: Amounts of time, money or distance viewed as a single unit take a singular verb.

options.why: A period of time ('Four weeks') treated as a single block takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.hint: Is "four weeks" four separate objects, or one single stretch of time?
questions.explanation: Expressions of time, distance or money (such as "Four weeks", "Ten miles", "Five thousand naira") are treated as one single unit and take a singular verb: "is".
questions.trap: Option B (are) tempts students because "weeks" ends in "-s". Ignore the plural "-s" when it names one unit of time.
questions.mnemonic: Time / Money / Distance as one block = singular verb (is).

askPresets.answer: 'Two hours is too long to wait' — one stretch of time, singular 'is'.
Even though 'weeks' has an -s, 'four weeks' here means one single period of time and takes the singular verb 'is', not 'are'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Neither Agbo nor his parents ______ the meetings now.

options.why: 'Now' signals present habit, not past 'attended'.
options.whyWrong: The time marker 'now' calls for present tense, not past 'attended'.

options.why: 'Parents' is plural and closer to the verb, so singular 'attends' does not agree.
options.whyWrong: With 'neither ... nor', the verb matches the nearer subject ('his parents'), which is plural.

options.why: 'Has attended' is singular and clashes with plural 'his parents' and 'now'.
options.whyWrong: Not only does 'now' favour simple present, 'has' is singular while 'his parents' is plural.

options.why: Under proximity concord, plural 'his parents' (closer to the verb) + 'now' takes plural present 'attend'.

questions.hint: Check two clues: "neither ... nor" matches the closer subject ("his parents"), and "now" shows present tense.
questions.explanation: With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here "his parents" is plural, and "now" points to the present tense, so we use the plural verb "attend".
questions.trap: Option B (attends) tries to agree with "Agbo" (or assumes "neither" always makes the verb singular), ignoring plural "his parents" right before the verb.
questions.mnemonic: Neither A nor B -> verb matches B (the closer subject).

askPresets.answer: 'Neither the boy nor his friends attend', vs 'Neither his friends nor the boy attends'.
'Attends' is singular, which would match 'Agbo', not the closer plural subject 'his parents'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Three-quarters of the church ______ painted by members the previous day.

options.why: 'The church' is a single building (singular), so three-quarters of it takes singular 'was'.
options.whyWrong: A fraction takes a plural verb only when the noun after 'of' is plural countable ('three-quarters of the chairs').

options.why: 'The church' is singular and 'the previous day' is past, so 'was' agrees in number and tense.
'The previous day' places the action in the past, not present 'is'.
options.whyWrong: The time phrase 'the previous day' requires past tense ('was'), not present ('is').

options.why: Wrong number and wrong tense: 'the church' is singular and 'the previous day' is past.
options.whyWrong: 'Are' is both plural and present, failing both subject agreement and past time.

questions.hint: With fractions like "three-quarters of X", look at X ("the church") to decide singular or plural, and check "the previous day" for tense.
questions.explanation: Fractions and percentages ("three-quarters of", "half of", "sixty per cent of") take their number from the noun after "of". Since "the church" is singular and "the previous day" is past, the verb is "was".
questions.trap: Option A (were) traps students because "Three-quarters" looks plural with its "-s". What matters is whether the thing being divided ("the church") is singular or plural.
questions.mnemonic: Fraction of [singular] = singular; Fraction of [plural] = plural.

askPresets.answer: 'Half of the cake was eaten' (singular cake), vs 'Half of the cakes were eaten' (plural cakes).
'Were' treats 'three-quarters' as plural, but a fraction of a single building ('the church') is still one part of a singular thing, so use 'was'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Measles ______ no longer impossible to manage these days.

options.why: Names of diseases ending in -s (measles, mumps, rickets) are singular and take 'is'.
Despite ending in -s, 'measles' is a single disease and takes a singular verb.
options.whyWrong: The -s in 'measles' is part of its name, not a plural ending; use 'is'.

options.why: Wrong number and wrong tense: 'measles' is singular and 'these days' is present.
options.whyWrong: 'Were' is plural and past, whereas 'measles' is singular and 'these days' means now.

options.why: 'These days' refers to the present time, not past 'was'.
