options.whyWrong: 'Was' is singular, but 'these days' requires the present tense 'is'.

questions.hint: Do not be fooled by the "-s" at the end of "measles" — how many diseases is measles?
questions.explanation: Names of certain diseases (measles, mumps, diabetes, rabies), academic subjects (mathematics, physics, economics) and games (billiards, draughts) end in "-s" yet are singular. With "these days" (present), "is" is correct.
questions.trap: Option B (are) treats "measles" as plural simply because it ends in "-s".
questions.mnemonic: Diseases/subjects ending in -s (measles, physics) -> singular verb.

askPresets.answer: 'Mathematics is fun' and 'Measles is preventable'.
'Are' treats 'measles' as plural because of the final -s, but measles names one single disease and takes 'is'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letters "ai" in: W_ai_ter

options.why: Waiter has the diphthong /eɪ/ (/ˈweɪtə/), the same vowel glide as flavour (/ˈfleɪvə/).
Cite has the glide /aɪ/ (/saɪt/), not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Cite uses the glide /aɪ/ (as in 'my'), whereas waiter has /eɪ/ (as in 'day').

options.why: Road has the diphthong /əʊ/ (/rəʊd/), not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Road glides to rounded lips with /əʊ/, unlike the /eɪ/ glide in waiter.

options.why: Hair has the centring diphthong /eə/ (/heə/), not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Hair ends toward the centre (/eə/), whereas waiter glides upward toward /ɪ/ in /eɪ/.

questions.hint: Say "waiter" slowly and match its first vowel (/eɪ/, as in "day") against the four options.
questions.explanation: In "waiter" (/ˈweɪtə/), the underlined "ai" is the diphthong /eɪ/. "Flavour" (/ˈfleɪvə/) has the exact same /eɪ/ glide in its first syllable.
questions.trap: Option D (hair) is also spelt with "air" like a vowel before "r", which makes some students think it matches "waiter", yet "hair" has /eə/ while "waiter" has /eɪ/.

askPresets.answer: Compare 'wait' and 'flavour' — both start with the /eɪ/ sound of 'day'.
Hair is spelt with 'ai', but the 'r' changes it to /eə/ (/heə/), whereas waiter has /eɪ/ (/ˈweɪtə/), matching flavour.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letters "ee" in: Fl_ee_

options.why: Flee (/fliː/) and field (/fiːld/) both have the long pure vowel /iː/.
Skate (/skeɪt/) has the diphthong /eɪ/, not /iː/.
options.whyWrong: Skate has the glide /eɪ/ (as in 'day'), not the long steady vowel /iː/.

options.why: Faith (/feɪθ/) has the diphthong /eɪ/, not /iː/.
options.whyWrong: Faith has /eɪ/, whereas flee has the long steady vowel /iː/.

options.why: Rid (/rɪd/) has the short vowel /ɪ/, not the long vowel /iː/.
options.whyWrong: Rid is short /ɪ/ (as in 'sit'), whereas flee is held long as /iː/ (as in 'seat').

questions.hint: Hold the vowel in "flee": is it short like "sit" (/ɪ/) or long like "seat" (/iː/)?
questions.explanation: "Flee" (/fliː/) has the long pure vowel /iː/. Among the options, "field" (/fiːld/) has the same long /iː/ sound despite its "ie" spelling.
questions.trap: Option D (rid) has a short vowel /ɪ/, trapping learners who do not distinguish short /ɪ/ from long /iː/.

askPresets.answer: Think of 'sheep' (/iː/) vs 'ship' (/ɪ/): flee and field match 'sheep'.
Rid has short /ɪ/ (/rɪd/), whereas flee (/fliː/) and field (/fiːld/) both use long /iː/.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letter "a" in: toler_a_ted

options.why: The underlined 'a' in tolerated (/ˈtɒləreɪtɪd/) has /eɪ/, matching stale (/steɪl/).
Kneel (/niːl/) has the long pure vowel /iː/, not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Kneel uses /iː/, whereas the underlined 'a' in tolerated sounds like 'rate' (/eɪ/).

options.why: Met (/met/) has the short vowel /e/, not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Met has a short steady /e/, while 'a' in tolerated glides as /eɪ/.

options.why: Mat (/mæt/) has the short vowel /æ/, not /eɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Although mat is also spelt with 'a', it is pronounced /æ/, not /eɪ/.

questions.hint: Read the third syllable of "tolerated" aloud: to-le-RATE-ed. Which word shares that vowel?
questions.explanation: In "tolerated" (/ˈtɒləreɪtɪd/), the underlined "a" is in the syllable "-ra-", pronounced /eɪ/. "Stale" (/steɪl/) has that same diphthong /eɪ/.
questions.trap: Option D (mat) is spelt with a single "a" like "tolerated", but the silent "e" pattern in "-ate-" gives /eɪ/ (as in "rate" and "stale"), not /æ/.

askPresets.answer: Drop the beginning of tolerated: '-rated' rhymes with 'stated' and matches 'stale' (/eɪ/).
Mat is spelt with 'a', but its vowel is short /æ/ (/mæt/), whereas tolerated has /eɪ/ (/ˈtɒləreɪtɪd/), matching stale.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letter "o" in: p_o_ster

options.why: Jotter (/ˈdʒɒtə/) has the short pure vowel /ɒ/, not /əʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Jotter uses short /ɒ/ (as in 'hot'), whereas poster has the glide /əʊ/ (as in 'go').

options.why: Counter (/ˈkaʊntə/) has the diphthong /aʊ/, not /əʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Counter starts wide with /aʊ/ (as in 'now'), unlike /əʊ/ in poster.

options.why: Heater (/ˈhiːtə/) has the long pure vowel /iː/, not /əʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Heater has /iː/, completely different from the /əʊ/ in poster.

options.why: Poster (/ˈpəʊstə/) and motor (/ˈməʊtə/) both have the diphthong /əʊ/.

questions.hint: Hear the first syllable of "poster" (/pəʊ-/) — it sounds like "post" or "go", not "pot".
questions.explanation: In "poster" (/ˈpəʊstə/), the underlined "o" has the diphthong /əʊ/. "Motor" (/ˈməʊtə/) has the exact same /əʊ/ glide in its first syllable.
questions.trap: Option A (jotter) looks similar at the end ("-ter") and also has "o", but "jotter" has short /ɒ/ while "poster" has /əʊ/.

askPresets.answer: Say 'go, post, poster, motor' — they all share /əʊ/.
Jotter has the short pure vowel /ɒ/ (/ˈdʒɒtə/), whereas poster (/ˈpəʊstə/) glides through /əʊ/ like motor.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letters "ow" in: c_ow_ed

options.why: Low (/ləʊ/) has the diphthong /əʊ/, not /aʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Even though 'low' is spelt with 'ow', it sounds like 'go' (/əʊ/), not 'cow' (/aʊ/).

options.why: Flow (/fləʊ/) has /əʊ/, not /aʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Like 'low', 'flow' is spelt with 'ow' but pronounced /əʊ/.

options.why: Cowed (/kaʊd/) and loud (/laʊd/) both have the diphthong /aʊ/.
Cooed (/kuːd/) has the long pure vowel /uː/, not /aʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Cooed uses /uː/ (as in 'food'), whereas cowed comes from 'cow' (/aʊ/).

questions.hint: "Cowed" comes from "cow" (/kaʊ/), not from "low" (/ləʊ/). Ignore the "ow" spelling!
questions.explanation: "Cowed" (/kaʊd/) has the diphthong /aʊ/, the same vowel sound as "cow" and "now". "Loud" (/laʊd/) has that same /aʊ/ sound even though it is spelt with "ou".
questions.trap: Options A (low) and B (flow) both use the letters "ow" just like "cowed", yet they are pronounced /əʊ/, not /aʊ/.

askPresets.answer: 'Cowed' and 'cloud/loud' share /aʊ/; 'low' and 'flow' share /əʊ/.
Low (/ləʊ/) shares the 'ow' spelling, but it glides from relaxed /ə/ to /ʊ/, whereas cowed (/kaʊd/) starts open with /aʊ/ like loud.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letter "s" in: confu_s_ion

options.why: In confusion (/kənˈfjuːʒən/), the 's' is voiced /ʒ/, matching the 's' in measure (/ˈmeʒə/).
Mission (/ˈmɪʃən/) has the voiceless sound /ʃ/, not voiced /ʒ/.
options.whyWrong: Mission has voiceless /ʃ/ (no throat buzz), whereas confusion has voiced /ʒ/.

options.why: Correction (/kəˈrekʃən/) has voiceless /ʃ/, not voiced /ʒ/.
options.whyWrong: The '-tion' in correction sounds like /ʃ/, without the voice buzz of /ʒ/.

options.why: Caution (/ˈkɔːʃən/) has voiceless /ʃ/, not voiced /ʒ/.
options.whyWrong: Caution ends with voiceless /ʃ/, whereas confusion has voiced /ʒ/.

questions.hint: Notice three options (mission, correction, caution) all have the voiceless "sh" sound /ʃ/. Feel your throat buzz on "confusion".
questions.explanation: In "confusion" (/kənˈfjuːʒən/), the underlined "s" represents the voiced consonant /ʒ/ (your throat vibrates). "Measure" (/ˈmeʒə/) has that same voiced /ʒ/ sound.
questions.trap: Option B (mission) also uses "s" in "-sion", but "-ssion" gives voiceless /ʃ/, whereas single "s" between vowels in "confusion" gives voiced /ʒ/.

askPresets.answer: Say 'measure', 'treasure', 'confusion', 'vision' — feel the buzz of /ʒ/ in your throat.
Mission (/ˈmɪʃən/) uses voiceless /ʃ/ (no voice buzz), whereas confusion (/kənˈfjuːʒən/) and measure (/ˈmeʒə/) use voiced /ʒ/.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letter "t" in: ter_t_iary

options.why: In tertiary (/ˈtɜːʃəri/), the underlined 't' is pronounced /ʃ/, matching 'sh' in shame (/ʃeɪm/).
In question (/ˈkwestʃən/), 't' is pronounced /tʃ/, not /ʃ/.
options.whyWrong: Question has the stop-and-release sound /tʃ/ (like 'church'), whereas tertiary has smooth /ʃ/.

options.why: Catch (/kætʃ/) ends with /tʃ/, not /ʃ/.
options.whyWrong: Catch ends with /tʃ/, whereas tertiary has continuous /ʃ/.

options.why: Chair (/tʃeə/) starts with /tʃ/, not /ʃ/.
options.whyWrong: Chair has /tʃ/, while tertiary has /ʃ/.

questions.hint: Notice B, C and D all have /tʃ/ (as in "church"). Say "ter-sha-ry" smoothly without a /t/ stop.
questions.explanation: In "tertiary" (/ˈtɜːʃəri/), the underlined "t" before "-iary" is pronounced /ʃ/ (a continuous hiss, as in "sh"). "Shame" (/ʃeɪm/) begins with the same /ʃ/ sound.
questions.trap: Option B (question) also has "ti" before a vowel, but after "s" it becomes /tʃ/, not /ʃ/.

askPresets.answer: Compare 'nation' and 'tertiary' (/ʃ/) against 'question' and 'chair' (/tʃ/).
In question (/ˈkwestʃən/), the 'ti' after 's' produces /tʃ/, whereas tertiary (/ˈtɜːʃəri/) has smooth /ʃ/, matching shame.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letters "th" in: Loa_th_

options.why: Breathe (/briːð/) has the voiced sound /ð/, whereas loath (/ləʊθ/) has voiceless /θ/.
options.whyWrong: Beware: the verb 'loathe' (with -e) has voiced /ð/, but the adjective 'loath' (no -e) has voiceless /θ/.

options.why: That (/ðæt/) starts with voiced /ð/, not voiceless /θ/.
options.whyWrong: In 'that', your throat buzzes for /ð/; in 'loath', only air passes for /θ/.

options.why: Loath (/ləʊθ/) and thaw (/θɔː/) both have the voiceless dental fricative /θ/.
Tank (/tæŋk/) starts with the stop /t/, not /θ/.
options.whyWrong: Tank stops the air behind the teeth (/t/), whereas /θ/ lets air flow past the tongue tip.

questions.hint: Look closely at the spelling: "loath" has NO final "-e", so it is voiceless /θ/, unlike "loathe" or "breathe".
questions.explanation: "Loath" (/ləʊθ/, meaning reluctant) ends with the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ (air only, no throat buzz). "Thaw" (/θɔː/) begins with that same voiceless /θ/ sound.
questions.trap: Option A (breathe) is a classic JAMB trap: words ending in "-the" (breathe, bathe, loathe) use voiced /ð/, whereas "loath" without "-e" uses voiceless /θ/.
questions.mnemonic: No -e in loath -> voiceless /θ/ like thaw and thin.

askPresets.answer: Compare 'breath' (/θ/) vs 'breathe' (/ð/), and 'loath' (/θ/) vs 'loathe' (/ð/).
Breathe (/briːð/) ends with a silent -e that voices the 'th' to /ð/, whereas loath (/ləʊθ/) has voiceless /θ/, matching thaw (/θɔː/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letters "dg" in: Lo_dg_e

options.why: Lodge (/lɒdʒ/) and soldier (/ˈsəʊldʒə/) both have the voiced affricate /dʒ/.
Rogue (/rəʊɡ/) ends with /ɡ/, not /dʒ/.
options.whyWrong: Rogue has hard /ɡ/ (as in 'go'), whereas lodge ends with /dʒ/ (as in 'judge').

options.why: Go (/ɡəʊ/) starts with hard /ɡ/, not /dʒ/.
options.whyWrong: Go has /ɡ/, unlike the /dʒ/ sound in lodge.

options.why: Measure (/ˈmeʒə/) has /ʒ/ (no initial stop), not /dʒ/.
options.whyWrong: Measure has smooth /ʒ/, whereas lodge starts the sound with a stop and release: /dʒ/.

questions.hint: Listen to "lodge" (/lɒdʒ/): it ends with the same /dʒ/ sound as "judge" and "jam".
questions.explanation: In "lodge" (/lɒdʒ/), the underlined "dg" represents the voiced affricate /dʒ/. "Soldier" (/ˈsəʊldʒə/) has that same /dʒ/ sound represented by the letter "d" before "ier".
questions.trap: Option D (measure) sounds similar to some learners, but "measure" has smooth /ʒ/ without the "d" closure of /dʒ/.

askPresets.answer: Say 'judge', 'lodge', 'soldier' — all three contain /dʒ/.
Measure (/ˈmeʒə/) has the smooth fricative /ʒ/, whereas lodge (/lɒdʒ/) and soldier (/ˈsəʊldʒə/) both have /dʒ/.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letters "gn" in: _gn_ash

options.why: Forge (/fɔːdʒ/) ends with /dʒ/, whereas gnash starts with /n/.
options.whyWrong: There is no /n/ sound in 'forge'.

options.why: In gnash (/næʃ/), 'g' is silent so 'gn' sounds as /n/, matching 'n' in new (/njuː/).
King (/kɪŋ/) ends with nasal /ŋ/, not /n/.
options.whyWrong: King ends with /ŋ/ at the back of the mouth, whereas gnash starts with /n/ at the gum ridge.

options.why: Ring (/rɪŋ/) ends with /ŋ/, not /n/.
options.whyWrong: Ring uses /ŋ/, not the /n/ sound of gnash.

questions.hint: Is the "g" in "gnash" pronounced or silent (like in "gnat" and "sign")?
questions.explanation: In "gnash" (/næʃ/), the letter "g" is silent, so the underlined "gn" represents simply /n/. "New" (/njuː/) begins with that same /n/ sound.
questions.trap: Options C (king) and D (ring) have "ng", tempting students who think "gn" sounds like "ng" (/ŋ/). Silent "g" leaves plain /n/.
questions.mnemonic: Silent g in gnash -> /n/ like new.

askPresets.answer: Remember 'gnat', 'gnaw', 'gnash' and 'sign' — the 'g' is silent, leaving /n/.
King (/kɪŋ/) has the back-nasal sound /ŋ/, whereas the 'g' in gnash (/næʃ/) is silent, leaving plain /n/ as in new.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters: Advantages

options.why: The final plural syllable '-ges' is unstressed.
options.whyWrong: English never stresses the final '-es' ending on advantages.

options.why: Advantages (/ədˈvɑːntɪdʒɪz/) carries primary stress on the second syllable: ad-VAN-ta-ges.
The prefix 'ad-' is weak (/əd-/), not stressed.
options.whyWrong: The first syllable 'ad-' is reduced to /əd/, while the main beat falls on 'VAN'.

options.why: The third syllable is weak /tɪ/, not stressed.
options.whyWrong: In advantages, 'ta' is unstressed; the strong beat sits on the second syllable 'VAN'.

questions.hint: Tap the four beats of "ad-VAN-ta-ges": the weak "ad-" leads straight into the big beat on "VAN".
questions.explanation: "Advantages" (/ədˈvɑːntɪdʒɪz/) has four syllables, with primary stress on the second syllable: ad-VAN-ta-ges (just like "advantage", /ədˈvɑːntɪdʒ/).
questions.trap: Option C (ADvantages) places stress on the weak prefix "ad-". Always listen for the reduced vowel /ə/ at the start.

askPresets.answer: Think of the base word 'adVANtage'; adding '-s' keeps stress on VAN.
The first syllable 'ad-' is pronounced weakly as /əd/, not stressed; primary stress falls on VAN (/ədˈvɑːntɪdʒɪz/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters: Intentional

options.why: Words ending in '-tion/-tional' place primary stress on the syllable just before '-tion': in-TEN-tio-nal (/ɪnˈtenʃənəl/).
The prefix 'in-' is unstressed; '-tion' pulls stress onto 'TEN'.
options.whyWrong: The strong beat sits just before '-tional', on 'TEN', not on 'IN'.

options.why: The final suffix '-al' is never stressed here.
options.whyWrong: Suffixes '-tion' and '-al' stay weak; stress sits on 'TEN'.

options.why: The final '-nal' is weak /nəl/, not stressed.
options.whyWrong: The last syllable is unstressed; '-tion' pulls stress to the syllable before it ('TEN').

questions.hint: Apply the "-tion" rule: primary stress lands on the syllable right before "-tion".
questions.explanation: The suffix "-tion" (and "-tional") pulls primary stress onto the syllable immediately before it. So "intentional" (/ɪnˈtenʃənəl/) is stressed on the second syllable: in-TEN-tional.
questions.trap: Option B (INtentional) puts stress on the prefix "in-". Remember that "-tion" almost always puts stress right before itself.

askPresets.answer: inTENtion -> inTENtional; eduCAtion -> eduCAtional.
The prefix 'in-' is unstressed; the '-tion' ending puts the main stress on TEN (/ɪnˈtenʃənəl/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters: Certification

options.why: Stress falls on the syllable right before '-tion' ('CA'), not 'FI'.
options.whyWrong: Words ending in '-tion' put primary stress on the syllable right before '-tion', which is 'CA'.

options.why: In a five-syllable '-tion' word, primary stress sits just before '-tion', not on the first syllable.
options.whyWrong: The first syllable may carry secondary stress (/ˌsɜː-/), but primary stress falls on 'CA'.

options.why: Words ending in '-tion' carry primary stress on the syllable right before '-tion': cer-ti-fi-CA-tion (/ˌsɜːtɪfɪˈkeɪʃən/).
The second syllable '-ti-' is weak, not the main beat.
options.whyWrong: In certification, '-ti-' is light /tɪ/; the strongest beat is 'CA' right before '-tion'.

questions.hint: Every word ending in "-tion" follows one golden rule: stress the syllable right before "-tion".
questions.explanation: All words ending in "-tion" take primary stress on the syllable immediately before "-tion". So "certification" (/ˌsɜːtɪfɪˈkeɪʃən/) is stressed on "CA": cer-ti-fi-CA-tion.
questions.trap: Option B (CERtification) catches students who hear the secondary beat at the start (/ˌsɜː-/) instead of the strongest main beat on "CA".

askPresets.answer: eduCAtion, inforMAtion, certifiCAtion.
The first syllable only has a lighter secondary beat (/ˌsɜː-/); the main primary stress sits right before '-tion' on CA (/ˌsɜːtɪfɪˈkeɪʃən/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters: Motivation

options.why: The second syllable '-ti-' is light /tɪ/, not stressed.
options.whyWrong: The '-tion' suffix pulls primary stress onto 'VA', not 'TI'.

options.why: The final '-tion' itself is never the stressed syllable.
options.whyWrong: Stress sits on the syllable BEFORE '-tion' ('VA'), never on '-tion' itself.

options.why: By the '-tion' rule, primary stress falls on the syllable right before '-tion': mo-ti-VA-tion (/ˌməʊtɪˈveɪʃən/).
'MO-' carries secondary stress, while the strongest primary beat is 'VA'.
options.whyWrong: Although 'mo-' starts clearly, primary stress in '-tion' nouns always lands right before '-tion' on 'VA'.

questions.hint: Count back one syllable from "-tion" — that syllable gets the capitals.
questions.explanation: Following the "-tion" stress rule, primary stress falls on the syllable immediately before "-tion". So "motivation" (/ˌməʊtɪˈveɪʃən/) is stressed on "VA": mo-ti-VA-tion.
questions.trap: Option D (MOtivation) copies the stress of "MOtive", forgetting that adding "-ation" shifts primary stress forward onto "VA".

askPresets.answer: Just like 'inVItation' and 'celebRAtion', 'motiVAtion' stresses the syllable before '-tion'.
MOtive has stress on the first syllable, but adding '-ation' moves the main stress to VA right before '-tion' (/ˌməʊtɪˈveɪʃən/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters: prohibition

options.why: Stress is on 'BI' right before '-tion', not on 'HI'.
options.whyWrong: In prohibition, 'hi' is weak (/ɪ/); the '-tion' suffix pulls stress onto 'BI'.

options.why: By the '-tion' rule, primary stress sits on the syllable right before '-tion': pro-hi-BI-tion (/ˌprəʊɪˈbɪʃən/).
Primary stress does not sit on the prefix 'pro-' in '-tion' words.
options.whyWrong: The first syllable may carry secondary stress, while the main beat falls on 'BI'.

options.why: The ending '-tion' itself is unstressed.
options.whyWrong: Primary stress sits right before '-tion' on 'BI', never on '-tion'.

questions.hint: Look at the verb "proHIbit" vs the noun "prohibition": "-tion" puts stress right before itself.
questions.explanation: For words ending in "-tion", primary stress lands on the syllable immediately preceding "-tion". Thus "prohibition" (/ˌprəʊɪˈbɪʃən/) is stressed on "BI": pro-hi-BI-tion.
questions.trap: Option A (proHIbition) keeps the stress on "HI" from the verb "proHIbit", forgetting that "-tion" moves the beat forward to "BI".

askPresets.answer: exHIbit -> exhiBItion; proHIbit -> prohiBItion.
The verb 'proHIbit' stresses HI, but adding '-tion' shifts the main stress forward to BI right before '-tion' (/ˌprəʊɪˈbɪʃən/).

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates: I left my bag on the TABLE.

options.text: Is the bag left under the table?
options.why: This contrasts 'on' with 'under', which would stress ON.
options.whyWrong: Stressing TABLE contrasts the piece of furniture/location, not the preposition 'on'.

options.text: Did I leave the shoe on the table?
options.why: This contrasts 'bag' with 'shoe', which would stress BAG.
options.whyWrong: If 'shoe' were being corrected, the capitals would be on BAG, not TABLE.

options.text: Who left the bag on the table?
options.why: A 'Who' question would put stress on I.
options.whyWrong: Stressing TABLE answers 'where?', not 'who?'.

options.text: Where did I leave the bag?
options.why: Stressing TABLE highlights the place, answering 'Where did I leave the bag?' (or contrasting it with another place).

questions.hint: Ask what question word or contrasting word replaces "TABLE" — "on the chair" / "where?".
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress falls on the word giving the key or contrasting information. Stressing "TABLE" identifies where the bag was left, so it answers "Where did I leave the bag?".
questions.trap: Option A changes "on" to "under" while repeating "table". Keep the stressed word out of the contrast if the question uses a question word like "Where".

askPresets.answer: 'I left it on the TABLE' answers 'Where did I leave it?'; 'I left it ON the table' corrects 'under'.
Option A changes the preposition ('under' vs 'on'), which would require stressing ON, not TABLE.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates: Kanu can play FOOTBALL.

options.why: A 'Who' question is answered by stressing KANU.
options.whyWrong: Stressing FOOTBALL answers 'what?', not 'who?'.

options.why: Stressing FOOTBALL supplies the sport Kanu can play, answering 'What can Kanu play?'.

options.text: What can Kanu do with football?
options.why: What he can do with it would stress PLAY, not FOOTBALL.
options.whyWrong: Stressing FOOTBALL answers what sport he plays, not the action 'play'.

options.why: The sentence gives no reason ('why').
options.whyWrong: Nothing in 'Kanu can play FOOTBALL' answers 'why?'.

questions.hint: Replace the word in CAPITALS with a question word: "Kanu can play WHAT?"
questions.explanation: When "FOOTBALL" carries the emphatic stress, it supplies the answer to "What can Kanu play?" while "Kanu can play" stays known.
questions.trap: Option C focuses on the verb ("do" vs "play"), which would stress "PLAY", not "FOOTBALL".
questions.mnemonic: Kanu can play FOOTBALL -> What can Kanu play?

askPresets.answer: 'KANU can play football' answers Who; 'Kanu can PLAY football' answers What can he do; 'Kanu can play FOOTBALL' answers What can he play.
Questioning what Kanu can do with a football would put the stress on PLAY, not FOOTBALL.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates: Aisha plays TENNIS always.

options.why: A 'Who' question would put emphatic stress on AISHA.
options.whyWrong: Stressing TENNIS tells us which game she plays, not who plays it.

options.why: This contrasts 'watch' with 'plays', which would stress PLAYS.
options.whyWrong: Here 'tennis' is repeated and the verb changes; that would stress PLAYS, not TENNIS.

options.why: Stressing TENNIS answers 'What does Aisha play always?'.
A 'When' question would put emphatic stress on ALWAYS.
options.whyWrong: Stressing ALWAYS answers 'when/how often?', whereas TENNIS answers 'what?'.

questions.hint: Cross out every option that repeats the stressed word "tennis" unless it is asking "what?".
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress on "TENNIS" highlights the sport Aisha plays, directly answering the question "What does Aisha play always?".
questions.trap: Option B repeats "tennis" and changes "plays" to "watch". That question would be answered by stressing "PLAYS", not "TENNIS".

askPresets.answer: 'AISHA plays tennis' -> Who? 'Aisha plays TENNIS' -> What?
Option B repeats 'tennis' and swaps the verb ('watch' vs 'plays'), which would require stressing PLAYS instead.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates: My house is ACROSS the road.

options.why: Changes 'my' to 'her' and omits the preposition, unrelated to ACROSS.
options.whyWrong: Changing 'my' to 'her' would stress MY, not ACROSS.

options.text: Is my room across the road?
options.why: Changes 'house' to 'room', which would stress HOUSE.
options.whyWrong: Repeating 'across' while swapping 'room' for 'house' puts stress on HOUSE.

options.text: Is my house on the road?
options.why: Contrasts 'on' with 'ACROSS', keeping 'my house' and 'the road' identical.

options.text: Is my house across the street?
options.why: Changes 'road' to 'street', which would stress ROAD.
options.whyWrong: Repeating 'across' and changing 'road' to 'street' puts the contrast on ROAD, not ACROSS.

questions.hint: Find the ONE option that replaces "ACROSS" with a different word while keeping everything else the same.
questions.explanation: In contrast-style emphatic stress questions, the matching option changes ONLY the word in capitals. Option C replaces "ACROSS" with "on" ("Is my house ON the road?" — No, it is ACROSS the road).
questions.trap: Option D changes "road" to "street" while repeating "across". Never pick an option that repeats the stressed word in a yes/no contrast question.
questions.mnemonic: Swap ONLY the capitalised word: on <-> ACROSS.

askPresets.answer: 'Is it UNDER the bed?' -> 'No, it is ON the bed.'
Option D repeats 'across' and swaps 'road' for 'street', which would require stressing ROAD instead.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates: HIS wife works in a bank.

options.why: A 'Where' question would put emphatic stress on BANK.
options.whyWrong: Stressing BANK answers 'where?', whereas HIS specifies whose wife works there.

options.text: Does his wife play in a bank?
options.why: Contrasts 'play' with 'works', which would stress WORKS.
options.whyWrong: Repeating 'his wife' and changing 'works' to 'play' puts stress on WORKS.

options.text: Does his concubine work in a bank?
options.why: Contrasts 'concubine' with 'wife', which would stress WIFE.
options.whyWrong: Repeating 'his' and changing 'wife' to 'concubine' puts stress on WIFE, not HIS.

options.text: Does my wife work in a bank?
options.why: Contrasts 'my' with 'HIS', keeping 'wife works in a bank' unchanged.

questions.hint: Find the ONE option that swaps "HIS" for a different possessive word while keeping everything else the same.
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress on "HIS" contrasts who the wife belongs to. Option D asks "Does my wife work in a bank?", swapping only "HIS" for "my" (No, HIS wife works in a bank).
questions.trap: Option C repeats "his" and swaps "wife" for "concubine". That question would put stress on "WIFE", not "HIS".
questions.mnemonic: Swap ONLY the capitalised word: my <-> HIS.

askPresets.answer: 'Is that YOUR bag?' -> 'No, it is HIS bag.'
Option C repeats 'his' and changes 'wife', which would stress WIFE instead of HIS.
